hints: Focus on the type of change in each equation, since forming bonds and bringing particles together releases heat while breaking them apart absorbs heat.
Notice that process 1 makes water from ions (neutralisation) and process 2 burns methane in oxygen (combustion), both classic examples that give out heat.
Consider what happens when a gas condenses to a liquid in process 3, as new intermolecular attractions form, then check if any process is left that needs heat in.
walkthrough:
**Remember what the sign means**

Think simply with your student hat on. A negative enthalpy change means exothermic, heat is released. A positive enthalpy change means endothermic, heat is absorbed.

$$\Delta H < 0 \text{ exothermic, } \Delta H > 0 \text{ endothermic}$$

**Check process 1 - neutralisation**

This is $\text{H}^{+}(aq) + \text{OH}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l)$. A new O-H covalent bond is made to form water, and bond making releases energy. This is the standard neutralisation, about $-57$ kJ per mol, so exothermic.

**Check process 2 - combustion**

This is $\text{CH}_{4}(g) + 2\text{O}_{2}(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2}(g) + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l)$. Burning a fuel always breaks some bonds but makes stronger $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ bonds. Much more energy is released than absorbed, so strongly exothermic.

**Check process 3 - condensation**

This is $\text{NH}_{3}(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_{3}(l)$. Gas particles are far apart and moving freely, liquid particles are close with hydrogen bonding attractions. Forming those attractions releases heat, so condensation is exothermic, the reverse of boiling which is endothermic.

**Put it together**

All three processes release heat, so all three have $\Delta H < 0$. That means none of them has a positive enthalpy change.

options.A: Correct. Process 1 is neutralisation (exothermic), process 2 is combustion (exothermic), and process 3 is condensation, gas to liquid (exothermic). All have negative enthalpy change, so none is positive.
options.B: Incorrect. Process 1 is often confused because ionic solutions look like bond breaking, but $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ join to make a covalent bond in water. Bond formation releases energy, so it is exothermic with negative, not positive, enthalpy change.
options.C: Incorrect. Students sometimes think breaking $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{O=O}$ bonds in combustion needs heat, so it must be endothermic. In fact the new $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ bonds release far more energy, so combustion of methane is strongly exothermic.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the common trap of mixing up boiling and condensing. Boiling, liquid to gas, is endothermic because attractions are broken. Condensing, gas to liquid, is the reverse and is exothermic because attractions form.
